The sunk cost effect is manifested in a greater tendency to continue an endeavor once an investment in money, effort, or time has been made. Evidence that the psychological justification for this behavior is predicated on the desire not to appear wasteful is presented. In a field study, customers who had initially paid more for a season subscription to a theater series attended more plays during the next 6 months, presumably because of their higher sunk cost in the season tickets. Several questionnaire studies corroborated and extended this finding. It is found that those who had incurred a sunk cost inflated their estimate of how likely a project was to succeed compared to the estimates of the same project by those who had not incurred a sunk cost. The basic sunk cost finding that people will throw good money after bad appears to be well described by prospect theory (D. Kahneman & A. Tversky, 1979, Econometrica, 47, 263–291). Only moderate support for the contention that personal involvement increases the sunk cost effect is presented. The sunk cost effect was not lessened by having taken prior courses in economics. Finally, the sunk cost effect cannot be fully subsumed under any of several social psychological theories.

In recent decades, a range of competing theories have been offered to explain why individuals sometimes persist in, or escalate commitment to, a suboptimal course of action because of prior investments of money, effort or other resources – i.e., the sunk cost effect. In evaluating these theories, it is important to identify scenarios in which they generate divergent predictions. We carried out 4 pre-registered experiments (N = 1,481) implementing two such types of scenarios: (1) waste-free scenarios, in which the resource is not lost but can be repurposed to a new goal; and (2) interpersonal scenarios, in which the decision-maker is not the individual who made the prior investment. Experiment 1 demonstrates that another individual's non-wasted effort significantly increases escalation of commitment. Experiment 2 shows that the other individual's prior effort can boost escalation of commitment even more than one's own. Experiment 3 provides evidence that the effect of others' prior investments may be driven by social expectations. Experiment 4 replicates the effect of another individual's prior investment while yielding no evidence that it makes any difference whether the initial decision was made jointly or by the other individual alone. Taken together, our findings challenge theories focused on waste aversion and self-justification, and highlight the complexity of ways in which social context shapes sunk cost reasoning.

The sunk-cost effect (SCE) refers to the continuation of an activity after investing resources in the activity. Current developmental research on the SCE in childhood is mixed, but some researchers suggest that sunk-cost judgments decline with age after childhood. To better understand age differences in sunk-cost judgments across the lifespan, we conducted two experiments with the widest age range used in the literature thus far to examine the SCE across the lifespan, while using the same measures for all ages. Samples ranged from 2 to 97 years of age (Experiment 1: lab-based, N = 682; Experiment 2: community sample, N = 378). We found a similar pattern across both experiments: Adults and adolescents consistently made sunk-cost judgments, but children did not. We also observed differences in age patterns between different sunk-cost measures, suggesting that researchers should consider how individuals of different ages might respond to different decision-making vignettes. Our findings suggest that children do not consistently make sunk-cost judgments like older children and adults.

The human mind is a mosaic composed of multiple selves with conflicting desires. How can coherent actions emerge from such conflicts? Classical desire theory argues that rational action depends on maximizing the expected utilities evaluated by all desires. In contrast, intention theory suggests that humans regulate conflicting desires with an intentional commitment that constrains action planning towards a fixed goal. Here, we designed a series of 2D navigation games in which participants were instructed to navigate to two equally desirable destinations. We focused on the critical moments in navigation to test whether humans spontaneously commit to an intention and take actions that would be qualitatively different from those of a purely desire-driven agent. Across four experiments, we found three distinctive signatures of intentional commitment that only exist in human actions: "goal perseverance" as the persistent pursuit of an original intention despite unexpected drift making the intention suboptimal; "self-binding" as the proactive binding of oneself to a committed future by avoiding a path that could lead to many futures; and "temporal leap" as the commitment to a distant future even before reaching the proximal one. These results suggest that humans spontaneously form an intention with a committed plan to quarantine conflicting desires from actions, supporting intention as a distinctive mental state beyond desire. Additionally, our findings shed light on the possible functions of intention, such as reducing computational load and making one's actions more predictable in the eyes of a third-party observer.

Young children anticipate that others act rationally in light of their beliefs and desires, and environmental constraints. However, little is known about whether children anticipate others' irrational choices. We investigated young children's ability to predict that sunk costs can lead to irrational choices. Across four experiments, 5‐ to 6‐year‐olds (total N = 185) and adults (total N = 117) judged which of two identical objects an agent would keep, one obtained at a high cost or one obtained at a low cost. In Experiment 1, adults predicted that the agent would choose the high‐cost object over the low‐cost one, whereas children responded at chance. Experiment 2 replicated these findings in children, but also included another condition which showed they were sensitive to future costs. They predicted that an agent would be more likely to seek out a low‐cost item than a high‐cost item. Experiments 3 and 4 then found that children do not anticipate the sunk cost bias in first person scenarios, or in interpersonal sunk cost scenarios, where costs are sunk by others. Taken together, our findings suggest that young children may struggle to understand and predict irrational behavior. The findings also reveal an asymmetry between how they consider sunk costs and future costs in understanding actions. We propose that this asymmetry might arise because children do not consider sunk costs as wasted.

The Interpersonal Sunk-Cost Effect

PSYCHOL SCI

Christopher Olivola Christopher Olivola

https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Christopher-Olivola

The sunk-cost fallacy—pursuing an inferior alternative merely because we have previously invested significant, but nonrecoverable, resources in it—represents a striking violation of rational decision making. Whereas theoretical accounts and empirical examinations of the sunk-cost effect have generally been based on the assumption that it is a purely intrapersonal phenomenon (i.e., solely driven by one's own past investments), the present research demonstrates that it is also an interpersonal effect (i.e., people will alter their choices in response to other people's past investments). Across eight experiments ( N = 6,076) covering diverse scenarios, I documented sunk-cost effects when the costs are borne by someone other than the decision maker. Moreover, the interpersonal sunk-cost effect is not moderated by social closeness or whether other people observe their sunk costs being “honored.” These findings uncover a previously undocumented bias, reveal that the sunk-cost effect is a much broader phenomenon than previously thought, and pose interesting challenges for existing accounts of this fascinating human tendency.

https://www.researchgate.net/publication/325099040\_The\_Interpersonal\_Sunk-Cost\_Effect

https://www.researchgate.net/publication/322102824\_Nonrepresentative\_Representatives\_An\_Experimental\_Study\_of\_the\_Decision\_Making\_of\_Elected\_Politicians

AM POLIT SCI REV

Lior Sheffer

https://www.researchgate.net/scientific-contributions/Lior-Sheffer-2067682193

Peter Loewen Peter Loewen

https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Peter-Loewen

Stuart Soroka Stuart Soroka

https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Stuart-Soroka

Tamir Sheafer Tamir Sheafer

https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Tamir-Sheafer

A considerable body of work in political science is built upon the assumption that politicians are more purposive, strategic decision makers than the citizens who elect them. At the same time, other work suggests that the personality profiles of office seekers and the environment they operate in systematically amplifies certain choice anomalies. These contrasting perspectives persist absent direct evidence on the reasoning characteristics of representatives. We address this gap by administering experimental decision tasks to incumbents in Belgium, Canada, and Israel. We demonstrate that politicians are as or more subject to common choice anomalies when compared to nonpoliticians: they exhibit a stronger tendency to escalate commitment when facing sunk costs, they adhere more to policy choices that are presented as the status-quo, their risk calculus is strongly subject to framing effects, and they exhibit distinct future time discounting preferences. This has obvious implications for our understanding of decision making by elected politicians.

It's only money

https://www.researchgate.net/publication/286491913\_It's\_only\_money

J PEACE RES

Charles Miller Charles Miller

https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Charles-Miller-4

Benjamin Barber

https://www.researchgate.net/scientific-contributions/Benjamin-Barber-2138734302

The sunk costs fallacy is an important concept in the academic and policy worlds. It has helped explain consequential national security decisions such as the escalation in Vietnam and the surges in Iraq and Afghanistan. While previous analysis of sunk costs in international relations has made no distinction between financial and human sunk costs, there is evidence in psychology that people treat human lives and financial costs differently. The consensus in the casualty sensitivity literature is that human sunk costs should lower support for a conflict, but there is as yet no evidence on whether financial costs operate in the same way. Using the Environmental Protection Agency's value of a statistical life to equalize human and financial costs, we create survey experiments through Mechanical Turk and GfK/Knowledge Networks about a hypothetical US military intervention to test if financial and human costs have the same effects on public opinion. We find that public reaction to sunk costs is contingent on the type of costs incurred. Consistent with the growing 'sunk costs skeptic' literature we find no evidence that any sunk costs induce greater commitment to a mission. Where the US contribution to the conflict is purely financial, sunk costs induce a desire to cut losses. When intervention involves US lives, sunk costs make no difference to the level of support. Finally, contrary to the implicit assumptions of past policymakers, ex ante levels of public support for sending troops and sending money are indistinguishable. These findings hold true both in situations involving high Iraq War level sunk costs and low Somalia-style costs.

https://www.researchgate.net/publication/286491913\_It's\_only\_money

J SPORT ECON

Quinn Keefer Quinn Keefer

https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Quinn-Keefer

The National Football League (NFL) draft is used to examine the presence of the sunk-cost fallacy in teams' playing time decisions. In the NFL, salary cap value represents a significant sunk cost to teams. We use the structure of the NFL draft to conduct a fuzzy regression discontinuity design. Optimal bandwidth local linear results suggest a 10% increase in salary cap value yields an additional 2.7 games started, for players selected near the cutoff between the first two rounds. Despite being no more productive, the first round selections receive a compensation premium, which leads to them starting significantly more games.

The Rationalizing Voter

https://www.researchgate.net/publication/255702288\_The\_Rationalizing\_Voter

Charles S. Taber Charles S. Taber

https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Charles-Taber

Milton Lodge Milton Lodge

https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Milton-Lodge

Human beings are consummate rationalizers, but rarely are we rational. Controlled deliberation is a bobbing cork on the currents of unconscious information processing, but we have always the illusion of standing at the helm. This book presents a theory of the architecture and mechanisms that determine when, how, and why unconscious thoughts, the coloration of feelings, the plausibility of goals, and the force of behavioral dispositions change moment-by-moment in response to “priming” events that spontaneously link changes in the environment to changes in beliefs, attitudes, and behavior. Far from the consciously directed decision-making assumed by conventional models, political behavior is the result of innumerable unnoticed forces, with conscious deliberation little more than a rationalization of the outputs of automatic feelings and inclinations.

This article builds on past framing research to probe the impact of casualty frames on the public's willingness to expend additional “blood and treasure” in an ongoing war. The rhetoric of “sunk costs” (often described as “sacrifices”) that must be redeemed through further conflict is a well-known, yet irrational, trope. Utilizing an experiment embedded in a nationally representative survey on attitudes about Iraq, we find that “investment frames” increase support for the war among individuals who believe the U.S. “did the right thing in Iraq,” but decrease support for the war among those who feel the U.S. “should have stayed out.” We also find, however, that framing effects are inconsistent when the frames are attributed to sources. These latter results demonstrate the importance of including unattributed frames to evaluate source effects in framing research.

Signaling Foreign Policy Interests: Tying Hands versus Sinking Costs

https://www.researchgate.net/publication/247517910\_Signaling\_Foreign\_Policy\_Interests\_Tying\_Hands\_versus\_Sinking\_Costs

J CONFLICT RESOLUT

James D Fearon James D Fearon

https://www.researchgate.net/profile/James-Fearon

The author distinguishes between two types of costly signals that state leaders might employ in trying to credibly communicate their foreign policy interests to other states, whether in the realm of grand strategy or crisis diplomacy. Leaders might either (a) tie hands by creating audience costs that they will suffer ex post if they do not follow through on their threat or commitment (i.e., costs arising from the actions of domestic political audiences) or (b) sink costs by taking actions such as mobilizing troops that are financially costly ex ante. Analysis of a game model depicting the essentials of each case yields two principal results. First, in the games' equilibria, leaders never bluff with either type of signal; they do not incur or create costs and then fail to respond if challenged. Second, leaders do better on average by tying hands, despite the fact that the ability to do so creates a greater ex ante risk of war than does the use of sunk-cost signals. These results and the logic behind them may help explain some empirical features of international signaling, such as many crises' appearance as competitions in creating domestic political audience costs. They also generate empirical puzzles, such as why the seemingly plausible logic of inference that undermines bluffing in the model does not operate in all empirical cases.

https://www.researchgate.net/publication/247517910\_Signaling\_Foreign\_Policy\_Interests\_Tying\_Hands\_versus\_Sinking\_Costs

The purpose of the present research was to gain greater insight into how people's support for an ongoing war might be influenced by providing information about recent casualties of war. On intuitive grounds, one might expect that such information might often decrease support for the war, especially when the war in question is relatively unpopular. However, research and theory on the “sunk cost effect” suggests, somewhat paradoxically, that highlighting such losses could actually increase, not decrease, support for the war, as driven by the goal to avoid wasting valuable resources. Across two experiments (one focusing on the war in Iraq, another focusing on the war in Afghanistan), we found that the effects of the war casualty information on attitudes were moderated by a recent use and activation of the relevant “don't waste” goal, which had been previously primed in a non-political context. The implications of our findings for theory and research on attitude change, as well as the judgment and decision making area, are discussed.

https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Jeffrey-Taliaferro

Great powers frequently initiate risky diplomatic and military interventions in the periphery—regions that do not directly threaten the security of a great power's homeland. Such risky interventions are driven by leaders' aversion to losses in their state's relative power, international status, or prestige. These leaders often persist in such courses of action even when they incur mounting political, economic, and military costs. More surprisingly, they undertake risky strategies toward other great powers in an effort to continue these failing interventions. Hypotheses concerning such interventions are derived from the prospect theory and defensive realist literatures.

James N Druckman James N Druckman

https://www.researchgate.net/profile/James-Druckman

Toby Bolsen Toby Bolsen

https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Toby-Bolsen-2

How do individuals form opinions about new technologies? What role does factual information play? We address these questions by incorporating 2 dynamics, typically ignored in extant work: information competition and over-time processes. We present results from experiments on 2 technologies: carbon-nanotubes and genetically modified foods. We find that factual information is of limited utility—it does not have a greater impact than other background factors (e.g., values), it adds little power to newly provided arguments/frames (e.g., compared to arguments lacking facts), and it is perceived in biased ways once individuals form clear initial opinions (e.g., motivated reasoning). Our results provide insight into how individuals form opinions over time, and bring together literatures on information, framing, and motivated reasoning.

Escalation and De-escalation of Commitment in Response to Sunk Costs: The Role of Budgeting in Mental Accounting

https://www.researchgate.net/publication/222476712\_Escalation\_and\_De-escalation\_of\_Commitment\_in\_Response\_to\_Sunk\_Costs\_The\_Role\_of\_Budgeting\_in\_Mental\_Accounting

ORGAN BEHAV HUM DEC

https://www.researchgate.net/scientific-contributions/Chip-Heath-2074875012

Research has traditionally assumed that people increase investment (or "escalate commitment") in response to previous investments (sunk costs). This paper presents several demonstrations which show that people will incorrectly de-escalate investment in response to sunk costs. I propose that people set mental budgets to control their resource expenditures: they set a budget for a class of expenses and track their investments against their budget. A lab study with real monetary incentives shows support for de-escalation and supports a specific rule for how people set budgets - based on the breakeven of total costs and total benefits. The budgeting process suggests that people are only likely to escalate commitment when they fail to set a budget or when expenses are difficult to track. The later part of the paper organizes the previous literature on escalation around these processes and provides additional experiments to illustrate each point. For example, I argue that previous demonstrations that have shown errors of escalation exclusively involve "incidental" investments that are difficult to track. A study in the current paper shows that people are more willing to invest time than money to salvage a monetary sunk cost and more willing to invest money than time to salvage a sunk cost of time, even when the time and money investments are of equal value. The paper concludes by discussing the rationality of escalation and de-escalation.

https://www.researchgate.net/publication/222476712\_Escalation\_and\_De-escalation\_of\_Commitment\_in\_Response\_to\_Sunk\_Costs\_The\_Role\_of\_Budgeting\_in\_Mental\_Accounting

It is commonly expected that individuals will reverse decisions or change behaviors which result in negative consequences. Yet, within investment decision contexts, negative consequences may actually cause decision makers to increase the commitment of resources and undergo the risk of further negative consequences. The research presented here examined this process of escalating commitment through the simulation of a business investment decision. Specifically, 240 business school students participated in a role-playing exercise in which personal responsibility and decision consequences were the manipulated independent variables. Anil K. Makhija Anil K. Makhija

https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Anil-Makhija

Experimental psychologists and decision theorists suggest that managers are overly reluctant to terminate economically unviable projects and that they fail to ignore sunk costs. This study serves two purposes. First, it shows that the framework of prospect theory allows us to reconcile the sunk cost effect with some older, well-established ideas in investment decision-making. Secondly, the study investigates the external validity of the sunk cost research in the context of the U.S. nuclear power program. The empirical analysis is based on share price movements in reaction to, among other events, all plant completions and cancellations (over $50 million) prior to March 1984. The results are mixed. However, prudency reviews ordered by Public Service Commissions around the nation point to evidence consistent with the sunk cost fallacy.

Daniel Kahneman 1934 – 2024

https://www.servsig.org/wordpress/2024/05/daniel-kahneman-1934-2024/

Guest article by Tor W. Andreassen.

Daniel Kahneman has stepped out of time, but his thinking will prevail

Daniel Kahneman (1934-2024) leaves an invaluable legacy in the fields of psychology and economics, deeply enriching our understanding of human thought and decision-making. His work, particularly alongside Amos Tversky on prospect theory, provides profound insights into human behavior, illustrating how individuals perceive gains and losses from a subjective stance, significantly influenced by loss aversion. This has vast implications across various domains, including marketing and public policy, where these insights can shape strategies for behavioral change.

In “Thinking Fast and Slow,” Kahneman sums up much of his research and unveils the dual-process theory of the mind, distinguishing between System 1's rapid, intuitive operations and System 2's slower, analytical reasoning. This dichotomy underlines the importance of recognizing our cognitive biases – such as the tendency to overweight initial impressions or underestimate costs and time – to enhance decision-making processes.

The advent of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Generative AI (GenAI) introduces new dimensions to Kahneman's foundational work, especially as discussed in his later book “Noise.” Here, Kahneman delves into the variability in human judgment and the potential of AI to mitigate biases and noise in decision-making. For service researchers, the integration of AI and GenAI technologies offers transformative potential in four key areas, enriched by Kahneman's legacy:

1. Enhancing Customer Decision-Making:

AI can help in designing services that reduce noise and bias in customer decisions. By analyzing large datasets, AI algorithms can uncover patterns in customer behavior that are not immediately apparent, leading to more personalized and effective service offerings.

2. Innovating Service Design through GenAI:

GenAI tools can simulate and evaluate countless service design scenarios, incorporating Kahneman's principles to identify designs that minimize cognitive load and bias. This enables the creation of more intuitive and satisfying customer experiences by leveraging predictive insights into customer preferences and decision-making processes.

3. Applying Behavioral Economics in Service Marketing with AI:

AI-driven analytics can refine behavioral economic models in service marketing, offering insights into how biases affect consumer choices. This can inform strategies that leverage psychological principles, such as framing effects and loss aversion, to influence customer behavior in more nuanced and effective ways.

4. Improving Healthcare Decision-Making:

AI and GenAI have the potential to revolutionize healthcare decision-making by providing tools that reduce diagnostic noise and enhance treatment personalization. By integrating Kahneman's insights into cognitive biases, AI applications can help healthcare providers make more accurate diagnoses and treatment recommendations, while also empowering patients to make better-informed health decisions.

Furthermore, the intersection of AI and Kahneman's work on “Noise” emphasizes the critical role of technology in identifying and mitigating inconsistencies in human judgment. As AI systems become more adept at recognizing and correcting for human biases, they offer a promising avenue for enhancing the accuracy and fairness of decisions in various service sectors.

Kahneman's exploration of noise and the potential of AI to counteract it invites service researchers to consider how these technologies can be leveraged to refine and advance our understanding of service delivery and consumption. His enduring contributions encourage a future where services are not only designed with a deep understanding of human psychology but are also augmented by the precision and insight provided by AI and GenAI technologies.

Tor W. Andreassen

Professor of Innovation at the Norwegian School of Economics

Research Fellow at DIG

Visiting Professor at IFM, University of Cambridge, UK

Abstract— This study investigates the phenomenon of

knowledge overestimation in the opposition's attitude towards quick counts in general elections in Indonesia. Involving 533 respondents in two studies, the findings of the first study indicate a significant correlation between subjective knowledge, objective knowledge, and the level of extremity in attitudes towards quick counts. These results reveal that individuals with extreme opposition attitudes tend to experience a discrepancy between the knowledge they claim to possess (subjective) and their actual knowledge (objective), depicting the Illusion of Explanatory Depth (IOED) phenomenon. The second study replicates and strengthens these findings, affirming those individuals with extreme opposition and belief in conspiracy theories about quick counts ("paid survey institutions") have lower subjective knowledge and higher objective knowledge. These findings support the hypothesis that extreme opposition attitudes towards quick counts are fueled by a gap between subjective and objective knowledge. The implications of these findings for public opinion on quick count results in the Indonesian political context are briefly discussed, on how extremity in political views and conspiracy beliefs can skew individuals’ perception and assessment of their knowledge.

Keywords— Illusion of Explanatory Depth, Political Extremity, Quick Count

I. INTRODUCTION   It is interesting to observe public attitudes towards science

in the political context, such as attitudes towards quick counts. Quick count, while not a scientific product per se, is related to science as it is a statistical method providing a rapid

estimate of election results. During the 2019 elections in Indonesia, there were accusations between presidential candidate camps regarding quick count results. Some politicians led public opinion towards distrust in science, especially social science. Public opposition to science is often attributed to the lack of public knowledge about science as were founded in \[1\]- \[3\].

Considering the developing level of scientific literacy in Indonesia, it is unlikely for the public to understand the workings/mechanisms of quick counts. Quick count itself is a relatively complex mechanism. To comprehend quick counts thoroughly, people need advanced knowledge of statistics that goes beyond basic statistical knowledge (e.g., understanding probabilities, sampling, margin of error, etc.). At the very least, people need basic knowledge of statistics to understand how quick counts work. However, it is important to note that increasing knowledge does not necessarily enhance positive attitudes or public acceptance of products resulting from scientific findings: some previous results \[4\] indicate that educational interventions targeting knowledge do not always increase public acceptance of science.

Individuals may feel they have in-depth knowledge about quick counts and hold extreme views against the results or use of quick counts, even if they do not know or have a limited understanding of statistics and probabilities. This means that increasing objective knowledge (science) alone is not always effective in changing public opinions about science. Individuals tend to form attitudes based on subjective knowledge (perceived understanding). For example, despite the Pew Research Center's findings \[5\]

indicating that genetically modified (GM) food is considered safe for consumption by the majority of scientists (88%), a cross-cultural study in the United States, France, and Germany in 2015\[6\] demonstrated that the extremity of public opposition to GM had a significant negative correlation with objective knowledge (measured by science literacy tests) but had a significant positive correlation with subjective knowledge (how individuals assess the depth of their knowledge about GM). In other words, those with extreme attitudes tend to express low-supported knowledge. Strong-extreme attitudes grow in alignment with perceived knowledge without necessarily being backed by scientific understanding.

Furthermore, this perceived knowledge is implicitly targeted by political elites to shape public opinion. Alter, Oppenheimer, and Zemla \[7\] found that opinion manipulation by political elites is assumed to have the potential to distort subjective feelings about how the public assesses their knowledge. When scientific products have consequences on political attitudes, such as the results of a quick count in general elections, extreme attitudes may also be influenced by political choices. In the context of quick count election results, public opinion and acceptance of quick count results \[or election results\] can be motivated by individual political attitudes such as conspiracy theories, partisanship, as found by Vitriol & Marsh \[8\] in preference for the losing candidate. Several studies \[8\],\[9\] also found that this condition is apparent in sample with low political knowledge.

Reference \[8\] especially highlighted that narratives built without data to lead to distrust in the opposition \[other candidates\] are widely discussed as conspiracy beliefs in the field of political psychology. It is known from findings of \[10\] that belief in conspiracy theories is based on individuals' motivation for order, structure, and clarity. This is because conspiracy theories provide simple explanations, protect preexisting beliefs, and feel consistent in explaining social and political events. Studies in \[11\] found that this kind of conspiratorial thinking are used to make sense of election results. If the candidate an individual supports loses in the election, belief in conspiracy theories gives individuals a way to cope with the unwanted fact without revising their expectations or preferences for that candidate ("the candidate I chose should have won"\[10\]). The connection between the illusion of understanding and conspiracy has been demonstrated in a US sample; it was found that individuals with low political knowledge, supporting a presidential candidate who lost in the election, having a high level of confidence in their understanding of political issues even when confronted with illusion of explanatory depth. Studies in \[12\]-\[13\] point out that people with this condition tend to not changing opinion even when failing to provide detailed elaboration of the issue mechanisms. Reference \[8\] also found that they are more likely to believe in conspiracy theories.

Conspiracy theories not only provide a way to cope with election results when the candidate loses but also have the potential to anticipate potential threats to individual preferences for candidates in the next election, assuming individuals still maintain conspiracy beliefs born in the previous election until the next election, and the candidate individuals choose in the next election comes from a similar

or the same partisan camp. In other words, there is a possibility that belief in conspiracy theories about the quick count in the previous election can trigger opposition attitudes towards the use of quick count. This is because both, the quick count results in the previous election and the use of quick count in the next election, are based on the same conspiracy theory. From this, the question arises: Do people who have opposition attitudes towards quick count results really have knowledge of how quick counts work? The assumption built in this study is that opposition attitudes towards quick counts (its use or results) are based on belief in conspiracies ("paid survey institutions"). Individuals who have extreme opposition attitudes or conspiracy beliefs about quick counts tend to have an overestimation of knowledge because they are motivated to do so: as the level of conspiracy increases/extremity of opposition increases, the gap between perceived knowledge and actual knowledge also increases. Conversely, the more people have moderate attitudes towards quick counts and low belief in conspiracy theories, the smaller the gap between perceived knowledge and actual knowledge. This is because there is no need for individuals to maintain deviant knowledge from science. A series of studies will be conducted to understand the pattern of dynamics of subjective knowledge, statistical knowledge (objective measurement), and extreme opposition attitudes towards quick count results.

This research explores the interplay between the extremity of political attitudes and the accuracy of self-assessed knowledge in the context of Indonesian general elections, particularly concerning opinions on quick count methods. Specifically, the study hypothesizes an interaction effect between the extremity of political views and the subjective versus objective knowledge of individuals. Hypothesis 1 (H1) proposes that this interaction manifests differently across the spectrum of political extremity: Hypothesis 1a (H1a) predicts a negative correlation between subjective and objective knowledge among individuals with high extremist attitudes, suggesting that stronger political biases may be linked to greater discrepancies between perceived and actual knowledge. Conversely, Hypothesis 1b (H1b) anticipates a positive correlation between these types of knowledge in those with low extremist attitudes, indicating that lesser political extremity could be associated with more accurate self-assessments of knowledge.

II. LITERATURE REVIEW

A. Illusion of Understanding

Knowledge is a prerequisite for having an attitude.

Individuals usually can only have an attitude towards something they know.

However, we can also have an attitude because we "feel" we know, where "feeling" knowing versus actual knowing (feeling vs possessing) are different. Feeling knowing is our self-assessment of how much knowledge we perceive to have, while actual knowledge is the degree to which we actually possess knowledge. This feeling of knowing will be further referred to as "perceived knowledge" because individuals essentially report the extent of their subjective judgment about what they know. Actual knowledge is

referred to as "science" because an individual's location is evaluated based on competency indicators (e.g., ability tests) that refer to objective criteria and standards.

People generally tend to overestimate their abilities, as evidenced by findings that students in the lower quartile on logical reasoning and grammatical skills tests often believed they performed better than 58% of their classmates \[14\]. The concept of Illusion of Explanatory Depth (IOED) describes the phenomenon where individuals overestimate their knowledge of complex systems or topics in more detailed sense. This overestimation occurs when people feel they have a detailed understanding, but upon explaining, they realize their knowledge is superficial. IOED is distinct from general overconfidence or superiority about one's position compared to others and is particularly notable in understanding causal systems rather than procedural, narrative, or factual knowledge \[13\].

Studies on IOED demonstrate that people often overestimate their knowledge of everyday objects like Wi-Fi, toilets, and bicycles (\[13\]; \[15\]). For instance, Rozenblit and Keil \[13\] found that participants initially believed they understood how a toilet works but revised their knowledge assessments after attempting to explain its mechanisms. This overestimation creates blind spots or gaps in knowledge about cause and effect. IOED specifically affects understanding of complex causal systems, such as artifacts (zippers, sewing machines, crossbows, toilets) and natural phenomena (earthquakes, waves, rainbows) (\[13\]; \[15\]), but tends not to occur with procedural knowledge (baking a cake), narrative knowledge (movie plot), and factual knowledge (capital city names) \[13\].

IOED extends to political knowledge. Alter, Oppenheimer, and Zemla \[7\] showed that participants' self-assessed understanding of political policies decreased after providing explanations. This decrease was consistent across party identifications and supported by objective evaluations. IOED can also be influenced by thinking styles; concrete thinking reduces susceptibility to IOED compared to abstract thinking (\[7\]).

Fernbach et al. \[12\] explored reducing political extremism by confronting overestimated knowledge of political policies. They found that asking individuals to write mechanistic explanations—detailing how policies work—encouraged moderation of extreme views. This approach highlighted gaps in understanding, reducing subjective knowledge and extremism. The change was mediated by increased uncertainty, as initial extremism was supported by unjustified confidence. Providing reasons rather than mechanisms reinforced extreme views (\[12\]).

In summary, IOED highlights the gap between perceived and actual knowledge, emphasizing the value of challenging individuals to articulate their understanding. This practice can foster more informed and balanced opinions, reducing political extremism and encouraging critical engagement with complex topics (\[6\]-\[7\],\[12\]-\[13\],\[16\]-\[17\]; contra \[18\]).

The Illusion of Explanatory Depth (IOED) occurs when people overestimate their knowledge. Overestimation affects people's understanding and promotes political extremism in both daily situations and political contexts. Research shows that when asked to justify policies, people typically realize they don't understand as well as they assumed. Engagement

with policy analysis reduces the gap between perceived and actual knowledge and challenging people's understanding helps promote more informed and balanced opinions and moderates political extremism.

B. Current Study

This study addresses the phenomenon of the "Illusion

of Explanatory Depth" (IOED), where individuals tend to overestimate their understanding of a concept or object, but when asked to explain in detail, they realize their lack of understanding. Studies note that IOED is not limited to technical or mechanical knowledge but can also occur in political contexts. Alter, Oppenheimer, and Zemla in \[7\] found that IOED occurs in political knowledge, and the manipulation of thinking styles (concrete vs. abstract) influences the extent of IOED. Furthermore, Fernbach, Rogers, Fox, and Sloman in \[12\] used this concept to reduce political extremism by asking individuals to mechanistically explain the policies they support, resulting in a decrease in political stance extremism and subjective understanding.

Firstly, this research notes that an increase in knowledge does not always have a positive impact on public attitudes towards scientific findings, as shown by some previous studies \[1\]-\[4\]. For example, public opinion on GM foods does not always align with scientists' views, indicating that subjective knowledge (feeling of knowing) does not always correlate with objective knowledge (science). The significance of this observation is translated into the Indonesian context, particularly regarding extreme attitudes towards quick count results in the electoral context. The research aims to explore whether individuals with opposition to quick count results truly have a deep understanding of how quick count works. This is especially relevant in the Indonesian political context, where public opinion can be influenced by politicians' statements and mutual accusations regarding quick count results. The main question of the research is the extent to which subjective knowledge, objective knowledge (statistical science), and extreme opposition attitudes towards quick count are interrelated and impact public perceptions of the validity and use of quick count in elections.

Three studies (includes preliminary) were conducted to explore the potential occurrence of IOED in the context of quick counts in Indonesia. A pilot study was carried out to confirm whether IOED occurs cross-culturally and with a sample of undergraduate students. If this illusion occurs in an academic setting, it should be more likely to occur in the general public. The first study is an attempt to replicate findings from \[6\], but in this case, the object of the attitude used is extreme opposition to quick counts in the 2019 elections. The research procedure and measurement tools will be designed as closely as possible to the reference study, with slight adaptations to the measurement context. The second study is an attempt to replicate the results of the first study, with a larger sample in the pre-2024 election context. This study is expected to provide insights into how we perceive public knowledge patterns and public acceptance of science often influenced by knowledge illusion biases.

C. Preliminary Study

The preliminary study of this research is an

experimental study with a one-group, pretest-posttest design and a single dependent variable (DV), which is the knowledge rating of how bicycles work. The independent variable (IV) in the study is the experimental sequence (preactivity of drawing bicycles = T1, post-activity of drawing bicycles = T2). A total of 99 participants (43 males, 56 females) within the age range of 18 to 25 were recruited, and all participants were students at the University of Indonesia. Participants were asked to determine the degree of subjective knowledge (T1) about how bicycles work on a 7-point scale (1 = I know very little/I don't know at all about how bicycles work, 7 = I have comprehensive knowledge about how bicycles work) before and after the activity of sketching bicycle schematics and answering multiple-choice questions about the location of the frame, pedals, and bicycle schematics. The bicycle drawing activity concluded with a reassessment of the knowledge level about bicycles (T2), and the wording of the T2 item was similar to the T1 question.

Fig.1. Illustration of Bicycles (A = 21 years, Female) (B = 20 years, Female) (C = 23 years, Male). A did not experience a change in understanding rating (pre 7, post 7). B did not experience a change in rating (pre 7, post 7). C experienced a change in rating (pre 7, pre 6). All three individuals own bicycles and can ride them. A and B made pedal position errors. Chain position and frame errors occurred in all three participants.)

The results indicate an effect of the Illusion of Explanatory Depth (IOED) treatment. Dependent sample t-tests were used to examine the average differences between T1 and T2. The bicycle drawing activity was found to successfully lower participants' subjective knowledge ratings, t(98) = 3.99, SE = .09, CI 95% \[.19, .56\], r = .37. The average subjective knowledge rating about bicycles declared by participants after the bicycle drawing activity (M = 5.44, SD = 1.07) was lower than before drawing (M = 5.82, SD = 1.21). These results indicate that mechanistic explanations reduce the overestimation of knowledge, and this reduction effect occurred across participant demographics (the majority of participants own bicycles). The authors also verified the success of the IOED treatment; participants were expected to report statements indicating metacognitive experiences. Some participant testimonials confirmed the effect of this activity: "I started thinking about the bicycle frame, instantly became confused about the bicycle's shape even though I already memorized and understood the bicycle a bit!", "Seems like I was wrong," "Initially felt confident and sure," "Didn't realize my understanding wasn't that accurate," "Turns out the knowledge I have is not as high as I thought." In general, this illusion phenomenon is experienced in everyday life objects.

Some readers might wonder about the relevance of IOED to a device (bicycle) compared to an object in a political

setting. The authors acknowledge that there are unlimited ways to explain what we know. Every explanation about an object has an indeterminate end state – there will always be a more detailed way to explain something (mechanical, molecular; \[13\]). Even with relatively simpler objects than political ones, participants who felt they provided a full explanation of the printer mechanism only estimated knowing about 30% to 60% of the total steps of how the printer works (study 7 of \[19\]). In essence, the nature of the dependent variable (DV) object is not influenced by the setting. Both device and political objects share a commonality in that they both contain mechanisms with explanations having an indeterminate end state

III. METHODOLOGY

A. Study 1: Extremity in the Result of Quick Count

The design of the first study adopts Fernbach et al.'s

(2015) study, operationalizing the Illusion of Explanatory Depth (IOED) as the correlation pattern between subjective knowledge, objective knowledge, and political extremism. The hypotheses for Study 1 are as follows:  H1:  There is an interaction effect between the extremity and the subjective knowledge of objective knowledge.  H1a:  There is a negative correlation between subjective knowledge and objective knowledge in those with high extremist attitudes.  H1b:  There is a positive correlation between subjective knowledge and objective knowledge in those with low extremist attitudes.

Method: Participant and Procedure

The first study involved 132 participants (Female N = 60), with various educational backgrounds: 60 high school graduates, 59 bachelor's degree holders, 9 master's degree holders, 2 diploma holders, and 2 junior high school graduates. The average age of participants was 22.80 years (SD = 3.67). Geographically, 59 participants were from DKI, 24 from West Java, 17 from Banten, 6 from Central Java, 5 from Yogyakarta, 5 from East Java, and the remaining 16 from outside Java. The majority of participants expected Presidential Candidate 01 to win in the 2019 Presidential Election (96 participants, with the remaining 36 expecting Candidate 02 to win). Overall, participants had an average level of concern about the quick count issue, scoring 4.73 (SD = 1.59) on a 7-point scale (1 = Not Concerned, 7 = Very Concerned).

Study 1 employed a correlational survey design with three measured variables: (1) extreme opposition attitude, (2) subjective knowledge, and (3) objective knowledge, specifically statistical knowledge. Age, gender, education level, and presidential choice were also assessed to provide a demographic overview. In testing hypothesis 1, only three

variables were included in the analysis. The outcome variable was objective knowledge. There were two predictor variables: subjective knowledge and extreme opposition attitude. Extreme opposition attitude was transformed into two categories (high and low) and used as a moderator variable. Scientific literacy variables were used to test the convergent validity of the objective knowledge measurement (statistics). Information about the total sample size, the number of data obtained and used in the analysis, is in the results section. Non-probability sampling was used as the sampling technique. Based on findings of \[20\] and \[21\], Covariates influencing the hypothesis testing in this context included gender and presidential choice.

Data were collected from April 25, 2019, to May 18, 2019, spanning eight days after the completion of the voting for the president, vice president, and legislative representatives. Initially, participants provided their consent to participate in the research. Subsequently, they were asked about their level of concern about the quick count issue on a 7-point scale (1 = Not Concerned, 7 = Very Concerned) on the same page. On the same page, the opposition attitude measurement tool for quick count results was also provided. On the third page, participants were instructed on how to fill in the subjective knowledge measurement tool according to procedure in \[13\]. Here, respondents were explained how a crossbow works and how to assess the level of knowledge based on the explained example of a crossbow object. After reading the instructions, respondents were asked to declare that they understood how to fill it, then fill in the subjective understanding measurement tool about quick count. On the fourth page, participants completed the scientific literacy test and responded to one attention check. On the fifth, sixth, and seventh pages, respondents filled in the basic statistics and probability knowledge test (the tool for subjective knowledge). On the eighth page, respondents provided demographic information (age, gender, education, political choice, and region of origin). The last page contained expressions of gratitude and a comment box for suggestions to the researcher. Participation in this survey was voluntary, and there were no questionnaire completion rewards.

Measurement

Extreme Opposition Attitude. Extreme opposition attitude

is operationally defined as the score measured from a single item assessing the attitude against the quick count results. The higher the score, the more extreme the individual's opposition to the quick count results. Extreme opposition attitude is measured by asking, "How much do you oppose the quick count results?" (1 = not opposed, 7 = extremely opposed) – adapted from \[6\] used in study 1).

Subjective Knowledge. Subjective knowledge is

operationally defined as the self-reported score indicating an individual's degree of knowledge about the quick count (\[6\],\[13\]). The higher the score, the more the individual perceives having a comprehensive understanding of the quick count. Subjective knowledge is measured by asking, "How well do you understand the mechanism/operation of the quick count?" (1 = shallow understanding, 4 = moderate understanding, 7 = deep understanding) – adapted from: study 1 of \[6\] and \[13\]).

Objective Knowledge: Objective knowledge is

operationally defined as the score indicating correct answers

on a test of basic knowledge about statistics and probability. The higher the score, the greater the individual's understanding of basic statistics and probability. Objective knowledge is measured by a 20-item test on statistics and probability adapted by the author. This test assesses the degree of basic knowledge in statistics and probability. Fifteen items are multiple-choice questions measuring knowledge of basic statistical concepts, and the remaining five items test basic knowledge of probability. The test is adapted from statistical quiz used in \[22\] and p.169 of \[23\]. An example item is, "There is a group of 10 people with an average height of 170 cm. Two people in this group have a height of 170 cm. If these two people are removed from the group, what is the average height of the remaining eight people?" (a = Less than 170cm, b = Not enough information to answer, c = Greater than 170cm, d = Same, 170cm). The test, scoring, and answer key are attached.

Scientific Literacy. Scientific literacy is operationally

defined as the score indicating correct answers on a test measuring an individual's knowledge of science in various domains such as physics, chemistry, genetics, and biology. The higher the score, the higher the individual's scientific literacy. Scientific literacy is measured by a test used in \[6\] with 15 true-false questions. This test assesses the level of individual knowledge in science across various domains like physics, chemistry, genetics, and biology. An example item is, "The Earth's core is very hot (True/False)." This tool is used as a test of convergent validity for the adapted objective knowledge test by the author.

Results and Discussion

Table 1 presents the correlation matrix among variables in Study 1. It can be observed that the subjective understanding of the quick count is not associated with an extreme opposition attitude against the quick count results (r = .01, ns). However, this extreme opposition attitude is negatively correlated with the actual understanding measured through the objective test of basic statistical knowledge and the objective test of scientific literacy. Individuals with an opposition attitude toward the quick count tend to lack statistical knowledge and have lower scientific literacy.

Regarding demographics, subjective knowledge is only significantly related to gender, where males have a higher understanding of quick count issues compared to females. The demographic variable that produces the most significant correlations is the choice of presidential candidate (capres). Compared to liberal presidential candidate supporters, those expecting a conservative presidential candidate to win tend to have lower basic statistical knowledge. From this, we identify a pattern consistent with the hypothesis direction, except for the subjective knowledge variable.

Hypothesis Testing and Results Interpretation

The first hypothesis was tested using Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression. Subjective knowledge was included as a predictor, objective knowledge as an outcome, and a dichotomous variable representing extremity categories was included as a moderator. Three covariates (presidential choice, gender, scientific literacy) were also included in the analysis. This analysis aimed to demonstrate the interaction between subjective knowledge and extremity level on objective knowledge. The results confirmed the proposed model (F(6, 125) = 8.06, p < .05, R2 = .28, MSE = 3.10). The interaction term between these two variables reached statistical significance (b = -.51, SE = .22, p = .023), although the main effects of extremity and subjective knowledge did not reach statistical significance. There was a significant increase in R2 by .03, F(1, 125) = 5.30, p = .02.

The alignment between subjective and objective knowledge occurred in those who did not hold extreme opposition towards the use and results of the quick count. Conversely, those who vehemently opposed the use and results of the quick count tended to exhibit a mismatch in knowledge assessments. In the context of this study, those who strongly opposed the quick count results were individuals who felt confident in understanding how the quick count works but lacked a grasp of basic statistics and simple probability concepts. H1, H1a, and H1b were accepted.

These results are consistent with the findings of \[6\]. Extreme opposition attitudes toward the quick count are supported by the metacognitive bias of IOED. Overestimation of knowledge occurs in those with extreme attitudes. Although the results of Study 1 confirm that the IOED phenomenon can also occur in the political context in Indonesia, this study only illustrates the pattern of relationships between variables in the context of the 2019 election. In Study 2, the author will replicate the results of the first study in the pre-election context of 2024 in 2023.

B. Study 2: Extremity in the Use  of Quick Count

Study 1 has several limitations related to the measurement

of variables. Firstly, it does not measure how conspiracy beliefs regarding survey institutions conducting quick counts, which should be a supporter of the validity of political extremity measurement. Study 2 aims to replicate the results of Study 1 and provide additional evidence on the measurement of extremity.

Participants and Procedure.

The dataset for Study 2 comprises additional data collected in October-November 2023, with a total of 401 valid respondents (N Female = 218). The average age is 24.20 years (SD = 8.77), ranging from 17 to 60 years. Based on the highest level of education, the majority of respondents are high school graduates (55.4%), followed by Bachelor's degree (30.9%), Master's degree (7.7%), Doctorate (3.0%), Diploma (2.0%), Junior High School (0.7%), and Elementary School (0.2%). In terms of academic disciplines, 44.9% are from Social Humanities, 10.5% from Exact Sciences, and 44.6% have missing data. The majority of respondents come

from Greater Jakarta (50.9%), followed by areas outside Greater Jakarta in Java (34.8%), and Beyond Java (14.3%).

About 46.9% were Liberal Presidential Election voters in 2019. The remaining 19.2% chose Conservative Presidential candidates in 2019, and 33.9% did not vote. When asked, "Will you choose a candidate similar to the one you chose before in the 2024 Elections?", 44.6% did not respond, 26.4% said "No," 14.7% said "Yes," and 14.2% answered "Not voting." Overall, respondents have an average level of concern for quick count issues at 4.78 (SD = 1.46) on a 7-point scale (1 = Not Concerned, 7 = Very Concerned). The data collection procedure is identical to Study 1, except we did not "train" respondents using a comprehension scale with crossbow exposure, and we used a different (smaller) number of items.

Measurement

Extreme Attitude Towards Quick Count Usage

Extreme attitude is operationally defined as the score

measured from a single item attitude against or in favor of quick count usage. The higher the score, the higher the individual's opposition to quick count usage. Extreme opposition attitude is measured by asking, "Indicate how much you oppose the use of Quick Count" (7 = not opposed, 1 = extremely opposed) – adapted from \[6\] used in Study 1.

Belief in Conspiracy Theory is operationalized as the

agreement score of respondents on the single item "The survey institutions conducting Quick Counts will always favor the candidate who finances them" (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree).

Subjective Knowledge of Information measurement tool

is the same as in Study 1.

Objective Knowledge of Information measurement tool is

the same as in Study 1. However, we only used 5 shorter and simpler items. The measurement tool is attached.

Scientific Information Literacy measurement tool is the

A bit different from the data analysis in Study 1, the data analysis for Study 2 will employ conditional process multiple regression to examine the interaction effect between subjective knowledge and extremity of attitude on objective knowledge. The predictor variable is objective knowledge, the moderator is the extremity of opposition to quick count usage in the 2024 elections, and the outcome variable is subjective knowledge. The covariates used remain the same, including gender, presidential election choice, and scientific

literacy. We are adding a few important covariates, namely age and education.

TABLE IV. INTERACTION BETWEEN OBJECTIVE KNOWLEDGE AND ATTITUDE

The linear regression analysis explores the relationship between objective knowledge (Objektif) and extreme opposition attitude towards quick count (Oppose), as well as the potential interaction between them (Obj x Oppose). The results indicate that objective knowledge does not have a significant relationship with opposition attitude (b = -0.03, p = 0.66). However, individuals with extreme opposition attitudes tend to have lower objective knowledge (b = -0.32, p < 0.01). There is a significant interaction between objective knowledge and extreme opposition (b = 0.13, p = 0.017), suggesting that the influence of extreme opposition attitude towards quick count depends on the level of individual objective knowledge. These findings support the hypothesis that, in extreme opposition, individuals may calibrate their knowledge depending on the extent of their objective understanding of the situation.

Control variables such as age, gender, presidential election choice, scientific literacy, and education level also contribute to the model. These findings provide deeper insights into the factors influencing objective knowledge, especially in individuals with extreme opposition attitudes towards quick count. The analysis shows that opposition extremity towards quick count is supported by the illusion of knowledge. When individuals have moderate views supporting quick count, the gap between subjective and objective knowledge tends to narrow. Conversely, in individuals with extreme opinions opposing quick count, the gap between subjective and objective knowledge tends to be maximal.

In other words, in extreme opposition, a phenomenon occurs where individuals tend to overestimate their knowledge. This aligns with previous findings supporting the claim that extreme opposition attitudes towards quick count

are supported by the illusion of knowledge (IOED). These results illustrate that individuals strongly opposing quick count may feel confident in their knowledge, but in reality, their objective knowledge is lower.

Thus, these findings provide empirical support for the hypothesis that extreme opposition towards quick count can be understood through the concept of the illusion of knowledge, where individuals tend to have greater confidence in their knowledge than is actually the case. This understanding enriches the literature on the dynamics of public opinion and depicts the complexity in individuals' perceptions of political issues, such as quick count in the election context. Figure 1 provides an overview of the pattern of the relationship between subjective and objective knowledge across levels of extremity in opposition attitudes towards quick count.

The linear regression analysis explores the relationship between objective knowledge (Objektive) and belief in conspiracy theory , as well as the potential interaction between them (Obj x Conspiracy). The results indicate that objective knowledge does not have a significant relationship with opposition attitude (b = -0.10, p = 0.33). There is a significant interaction between objective knowledge and belief in conspiracy theory (b = -0.16, p = 0.01), suggesting that the

influence of belief in conspiracy theory depends on the level of individual objective knowledge. These findings support the hypothesis that, in high belief conspiracy theory, individuals may miscalibrated their knowledge depending on the extent of their objective understanding of the situation.

CONSPIRACY BELIEF

Fig. 3. Overestimation of Knowledge across Levels of Belief in Conspiracy

Theory. (In conditions of extreme opposition to the use of quick count, the higher the subjective knowledge, the lower the objective knowledge. Conspiracy = belief in conspiracy theory based on -1, 0, +1 SD, "The survey institutions conducting Quick Counts will always favor the candidate who finances them.")

The slope of each line indicates that individuals with high extremity in their opposition to quick counts believe they understand the system much better than they actually do, as reflected by their lower scores in objective knowledge assessments. This misalignment is less pronounced in individuals with moderate and low extremity, suggesting that as individuals become more extreme in their views, they are likely to overestimate their understanding more significantly. This phenomenon is a classic demonstration of the Illusion of Explanatory Depth (IOED), where confidence in one's knowledge increases despite a lack of supporting factual understanding. For individuals with high extremity/conspiracy in their views, their inflated confidence in their misunderstood knowledge could lead to more rigid and polarized stances due to miscalibration of knowledge. Those with moderate to low extremity/conspiracy show a closer alignment between their subjective and objective knowledge, suggesting that their beliefs and opinions might be more calibrated: malleable and open to adjustment upon receiving new or clarifying information

IV. DISCUSSION OF RESULTS This research aimed to replicate Fernbach, Light, Scott,

Inbar, and Rozin study \[6\] to understand the underpinnings of opposition attitudes towards outcomes (Study 1) and usage

(Study 2) of quick counts in general elections. The analysis results indicate that extreme opposition to quick count in the election context is likely supported by the illusion of knowledge (IOED). Individuals with extreme opposition views tend to have a maximal gap between their subjective and objective knowledge. This finding consistently supports the hypothesis that extreme opposition attitudes toward quick count can be explained through metacognitive bias, where individuals tend to overestimate their understanding of the quick count process.

High subjective knowledge, especially in those vehemently opposing quick count, does not always reflect accurate objective understanding. In fact, there is a significant gap between individuals' beliefs in their knowledge and the reality of objective knowledge. These results confirm previous findings that extreme attitudes are associated with the illusion of IOED previously found in \[6\], \[7\], and \[12\], providing a deeper understanding of the mechanisms underlying political beliefs and views. Control variables such as age, gender, previous presidential election choice, scientific literacy, and education level also significantly contribute to prediction model.

However, it should be acknowledged that this study has limitations, including the generalization of findings only to the 2019 election context and the use of Study 2 data as additional data. Regarding respondent demographics, it is essential to note that the majority of respondents in Study 2 are a group of first-time eligible voters. This condition implies that most of this group has limited exposure or has not been significantly exposed to political opposition extremity. Thus, these limitations suggest that interpreting findings should be done with an understanding that respondents' perceptions may not fully reflect the extremeness in political attitudes and opinions. Therefore, further research with broader coverage and population may provide a more comprehensive understanding. This condition implies that most of them have not experienced or been significantly exposed to political opposition extremity. Therefore, this limitation indicates that the interpretation of findings should be done with an understanding that respondents' views and perceptions may not fully represent the variation or extremeness in political opinions.

Furthermore, creating spaces for open dialogue and discussion can help individuals confront and question their beliefs, allowing for a more nuanced understanding. Facilitating community forums or online platforms where people can engage with experts and peers to discuss political and scientific issues can promote a culture of inquiry and reduce reliance on simplistic explanations offered by conspiracy theories. Encouraging individuals to seek out twosided information, which involves considering multiple perspectives on an issue, can lead to a more balanced understanding and reduce the polarization caused by conspiracy theories. Empowering individuals to seek out credible sources and verify information can significantly diminish the impact of conspiracy narratives \[24\]\[25\].

V. CONCLUSION, IMPLICATIONS AND FUTURE AGENDA This study illustrates the relationship between individuals'

subjective knowledge and their objective knowledge as influenced by varying degrees of belief in conspiracy

theories. The result shows that as the belief in conspiracy theories increases—from low to high—the subjective knowledge reported by individuals also increases. Conversely, their objective knowledge decreases, indicating a significant overestimation of their understanding of the subject matter.

We can conclude that there is a illusion of explanatory depth (IOED) among those who strongly believe in conspiracy theories. This illusion leads them to think they understand complex systems such as quick counts far more than they actually do, while their actual understanding, as measured objectively, is quite limited. This overestimation of knowledge may impact more extreme opposition to usage of science within public sphere \[6\], as individuals are less likely to seek out or accept information that contradicts their inflated perception of their own understanding.

It is important to note that this study has limitations, such as focusing on the 2019 election and a specific population. Future research should expand the scope of investigation to include multiple elections and diverse population groups to provide a more comprehensive understanding of IOED and conspiracy within the Indonesian political context. Longitudinal studies could also provide valuable information on how IOED and related cognitive biases evolve over time and interact with political attitudes, identifying critical intervention points for fostering more informed and balanced political views. Moreover, future studies could examine the role of digital and social media in disseminating misinformation and conspiracy theories, analyzing how these platforms contribute to or mitigate the effects of IOED. Understanding the dynamics of information spread in the digital age can inform strategies to promote accurate information dissemination and enhance public engagement with credible sources \[24\]\[25\].

This study is critical for addressing misinformation and designing educational interventions aimed at reducing political extremism. It emphasizes the importance of strategies that not only provide factual information but also actively work to recalibrate individuals' perceptions of their own knowledge. Engaging people in explaining their understanding in detail can expose the gaps in their knowledge and potentially reduce the extremity of their views by aligning their subjective knowledge more closely with their objective knowledge. This approach could be particularly effective in mitigating the influence of conspiracy theories by demonstrating the complexity of the issues at hand and revealing the oversimplifications that such theories often rely on.

Title: Heuristics and Behaviorial Decision Making: Theory Evidence and Applications – First

Authors: Dimitrios Thomakos

Cover Design: Panagiotis Xanthis

To all students and researchers

who dare to question conventional wisdom

and seek deeper understanding

of human judgment and decision-making

This monograph represents a comprehensive treatment of heuristics and behavioral decision-

making, synthesizing more than six decades of groundbreaking research that has funda-

mentally transformed our understanding of human judgment, choice, and rationality.

The work you hold in your hands is designed as both a teaching text for advanced under-

graduate and graduate courses and as a reference volume for researchers in psychology,

economics, artificial intelligence, and related fields.

The study of heuristics and biases emerged from a profound dissatisfaction with clas-

sical models of human rationality. For centuries, economic and philosophical traditions

assumed that human beings approximate the ideal of Homo Economicus—a perfectly

rational agent who possesses complete information, unlimited computational capacity,

and stable, well-ordered preferences. This idealized model, while mathematically elegant,

failed to account for systematic patterns of human behavior observed in both laboratory

experiments and real-world decision contexts.

The pioneering contributions of Herbert Simon, Daniel Kahneman, Amos Tversky,

and Richard Thaler—recognized by four Nobel Prizes in Economic Sciences (1978, 2002,

and 2017)—demolished the classical rationality paradigm and replaced it with a richer,

more psychologically realistic understanding of human decision-making. Their research

demonstrated that human cognition is characterized by bounded rationality: system-

atic limitations in attention, memory, and computational capacity that lead decision-

makers to rely on mental shortcuts or heuristics. While these heuristics enable effi-

cient judgment under uncertainty, they also produce predictable and systematic biases—

deviations from normative standards of logic, probability theory, and rational choice.

Structure and Scope

#### This monograph is organized into eight major parts comprising 25 chapters:

Part I: Foundations establishes the historical and theoretical context, examining

the classical rationality paradigm and Herbert Simon’s revolutionary concept of bounded

rationality.

Part II: The Three Primary Heuristics provides detailed treatment of represen-

tativeness, availability, and anchoring-and-adjustment—the three foundational heuristics

identified by Kahneman and Tversky in their seminal 1974 Science paper.

Part III: Extensions and Related Theories explores prospect theory, mental

accounting, and the extensive catalog of additional cognitive biases documented in sub-

sequent research.

Part IV: Dual-Process Theories examines the System 1/System 2 framework that

distinguishes automatic, intuitive processing from deliberate, analytical reasoning.

Part V: Debiasing and Interventions surveys evidence-based techniques for re-

ducing cognitive biases at individual, structural, and organizational levels.

Part VI: Applications demonstrates how insights from behavioral decision research

inform policy design, business strategy, medical practice, legal judgment, and artificial

intelligence.

Part VII: Advanced Topics and Frontiers engages with ecological rationality,

neuroscientific foundations, cross-cultural research, and intertemporal choice.

Part VIII: Synthesis and Future Directions integrates multiple theoretical per-

spectives and identifies promising directions for future research.

A distinctive feature of this monograph is Chapter 11, which examines oracle-based de-

cision systems—from ancient tarot and Delphic oracles to modern randomization devices.

This chapter demonstrates how even seemingly non-rational practices can be rigorously

analyzed using Bayesian frameworks and decision theory, revealing their potential in-

strumental value for preference discovery, commitment, and breaking decision paralysis.

This material illustrates the breadth of behavioral decision science and its capacity to

illuminate diverse judgment phenomena.

Pedagogical Approach

#### This monograph is designed for active learning. Each chapter includes:

 Clear definitions of key concepts, highlighted in colored boxes

 Classic experimental demonstrations that reveal the operation of heuristics

 Mathematical formalizations where appropriate

 Empirical evidence summaries reviewing the state of research

 Real-world applications connecting theory to practice

 Discussion questions to stimulate critical thinking (in teaching supplements)

The monograph assumes familiarity with undergraduate-level statistics and research

methods but does not require advanced mathematical training. Technical material is

presented accessibly, with intuitive explanations preceding formal treatments.

Acknowledgments

This work would not have been possible without the intellectual contributions of countless

researchers who have advanced the field of behavioral decision science over the past six

decades. I am particularly indebted to the foundational work of Herbert Simon, Daniel

Kahneman, Amos Tversky, Richard Thaler, Paul Slovic, Baruch Fischhoff, Sarah Licht-

enstein, Gerd Gigerenzer, Eldar Shafir, and many others whose research is synthesized

I thank my interns Panagiotis Xanthis and Paris Vlachos at the Cybernetics and

Artificial Intelligence Laboratory for their thoughtful questions, constructive criticism,

and enthusiastic engagement with these ideas. Their curiosity and insight have shaped

my understanding and improved this work immeasurably. I also express my appreciation

to my Ph.D. student Konstantinos Papadimitriou for his excellent research assistance and

throughtful comments on this project.

I hope this monograph serves as both a comprehensive introduction for students and

a useful reference for researchers and practitioners seeking to apply behavioral insights

to real-world problems.

Dimitrios Thomakos

Athens, Greece

January 2026
